How notebook cells work

A notebook is a list of cells. When you run a cell, the variables it creates stay in memory (the kernel) so later cells can use them. Two things follow from that:

  • Order matters, not position. If cell 3 uses df and you never ran cell 2, you get a NameError. The number in brackets next to a cell, like [4], tells you the order it actually ran in.
  • The last line prints itself. If the last line of a cell is a value, such as df.head(), the notebook shows it as a nice table without print(). In this course we use print() so the output matches the text exactly.

Tip

When something feels broken, use Runtime → Restart session and run all (Colab) or Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells (JupyterLab). This clears memory and runs everything top to bottom, which is exactly how someone else would run your notebook.

Suppose a classmate says their tumor classifier is 63% accurate. Is that good? On the breast cancer dataset bundled with scikit-learn, a "model" that ignores every measurement and always answers "benign" scores about 63%. So their model may have learned nothing at all. This week is about making sure you can tell the difference.

The supervised learning workflow

You trained a first model before this course. Here is that same process written out as the five steps we will use, and improve, all term:

  1. Load the data into features X (the inputs) and labels y (the answers).
  2. Split it into a training set and a test set.
  3. Fit a model on the training set only.
  4. Predict on the test set, which the model has never seen.
  5. Evaluate by comparing predictions with the true test labels.

In this dataset, label 1 means benign and 0 means malignant. Two of the first ten predictions are wrong. Training accuracy is higher than test accuracy, which is normal: the model has already seen the training rows. Only the test number tells you how the model will do on new patients.

model.score(X, y) is a shortcut. For classifiers it computes accuracy, exactly like accuracy_score(y, model.predict(X)).

Why we split at all

A model is only useful on data it hasn't seen yet. If you score it on the same rows it trained on, you are grading a student with the exact questions they studied. A deep enough decision tree can memorize every training row and score 100% there while doing worse on new rows.

The test set is your stand-in for the future. Treat it like a sealed exam:

  • Don't fit anything on it: not the model, and (next week) not the scaler or imputer either.
  • Don't keep tweaking your model until the test score looks good. If you do, the test set quietly becomes training data. In week 4 you'll learn cross-validation, which lets you compare choices without touching the test set.

The arguments that matter

  • test_size=0.25: hold out 25% of rows. Anything from 0.2 to 0.3 is typical for small datasets.
  • random_state=42: the split is random. Fixing the seed makes it the same every run and on every computer, so your results can be reproduced. The number itself means nothing; 0 and 42 are just habits.
  • stratify=y: keep the class proportions the same in train and test.

Stratify: keeping the classes balanced across the split

Without stratify, a random split can give the test set noticeably more or fewer of one class than the full dataset has. With small test sets this happens a lot:

Because the labels are 0s and 1s, y.mean() is the share of 1s. The plain splits swing from 59.6% to 68.4% benign depending on luck. The stratified splits stay at the dataset's rate every time. Use stratify=y for classification unless you have a reason not to. (You can't stratify a regression target directly, since every value is different.)

Baselines: the score to beat

A baseline is the score you get with no real learning. If your model can't beat it, the model isn't useful, no matter how impressive the number looks.

scikit-learn's DummyClassifier gives you baselines that fit and score exactly like real models:

most_frequent looks only at y_train, finds the most common class (benign), and predicts it for every row. It completely ignores X. That alone gets 62.9%. The tree's 94.4% is a real improvement, because it cuts the error rate from about 37% to about 6%.

Other strategies:

  • strategy="stratified": guesses randomly, in proportion to the training classes.
  • strategy="uniform": guesses every class with equal chance.
  • strategy="constant", constant=0: always predicts the class you name.

For regression, DummyRegressor(strategy="mean") predicts the training average for every row:

Mean absolute error (MAE) is the average size of a prediction's miss, in the target's units (here, a disease-progression score). Lower is better. The linear model's typical miss is about 24 points smaller than guessing the average.

Watch out

High accuracy on its own means nothing. When 95% of emails are not spam, a filter that never flags anything is 95% accurate and completely useless. Always print the baseline next to your model's score.

What usually goes wrong

  • Fitting on everything, then splitting. The test rows have already influenced the model, so the score is too optimistic.
  • Forgetting random_state. Your score changes every run, and you can't tell whether a change you made helped or you just got a luckier split.
  • Comparing models on different splits. Use the same X_train/X_test for every model you compare.
  • Skipping the baseline. Do it every time. It takes three lines.

The split happens once, before any model exists. Every candidate below uses these exact four variables.

The function returns a dictionary rather than printing. A list of dictionaries turns straight into a pandas table in the next step.

We record training accuracy too. A large gap between train and test is an early sign of overfitting, which you'll study properly in week 4.

Read it row by row:

  • stratified and uniform guess randomly, so they score around one in three. They need a random_state too, or their score changes every run.
  • k-NN clearly beats the baselines but trails the tree. k-NN measures distance between rows, and wine features have very different scales (proline runs into the hundreds and beyond, while hue stays near 1), so one feature dominates. You'll fix exactly this with scaling next week.

The question that matters is "how much better than doing nothing?" Add a column for that:

Step 5: Does the ranking survive a different split?

A test set of 45 rows is small. One or two lucky rows move accuracy by more than 2 points. So rerun the comparison over ten different splits:

Three things to notice:

Real datasets arrive with blanks, text labels, and columns measured in wildly different units. scikit-learn models refuse all three: hand LogisticRegression a single NaN or the string "north" and fit crashes. This week you fix the data, and you learn the rule that keeps the fixes honest: every preparation step learns from the training set only.

Setting up a messy dataset

The bundled datasets are clean, so we'll dirty one on purpose. Run these cells in order in one notebook; later cells use variables from earlier ones.

df.isna().sum() is the first thing to run on any new dataset. It counts blanks per column. Notice that we split before fixing anything. That ordering is the whole point of this week.

Cleaning: drop or fill?

df.dropna() would delete 63 rows, about 11% of the data, to fix blanks in only three columns. Dropping is fine when very few rows are affected. It is risky when blanks aren't random. For example, if one clinic's machine often fails to record texture, dropping those rows removes that clinic's patients, and your model learns less about them.

Other cleaning to check before modeling: duplicate rows (df.duplicated().sum()), numbers stored as text (df.dtypes shows object), and impossible values such as a negative radius.

Filling blanks with SimpleImputer

SimpleImputer replaces each blank with a value learned from the data:

Every scikit-learn preprocessing tool works the same way:

  • fit learns something from data (here, each column's median) and stores it in an attribute ending in _.
  • transform applies what was learned to any data.

Test blanks get filled with the training median. That's how it works in real use: when a new patient arrives, you only have the numbers you learned in the past.

Strategies: "mean" and "median" for numbers (median is safer when there are outliers), "most_frequent" for categories, and "constant" with fill_value= for a fixed value like "unknown".

Encoding categories with OneHotEncoder

Models need numbers. Replacing north/south/east with 0/1/2 invents a fake order (is east "twice" south?). One-hot encoding makes one 0/1 column per category instead:

south becomes [0, 0, 1]. west never appeared during fit, so with handle_unknown="ignore" it becomes all zeros instead of crashing. Always set this. Some category will eventually show up at prediction time that training never saw. (sparse_output=False just makes the output printable; inside a pipeline you can leave it out.)

Scaling with StandardScaler

StandardScaler subtracts each column's training mean and divides by its standard deviation, so every feature ends up centered on 0 with spread 1. (The -0.00 is a tiny rounding error, not a bug.) It matters for models that compare distances or weights across features: k-NN, logistic regression, SVMs. Trees split one feature at a time and don't care about scale.

Putting it together: ColumnTransformer and Pipeline

Different columns need different steps. ColumnTransformer routes each group of columns to its own steps, and Pipeline chains preparation with a model:

One model.fit(X_train, y_train) call fits every imputer, scaler, and encoder on training rows only, then trains the classifier. One model.score(X_test, y_test) call transforms the test rows with what was learned and predicts. You can't accidentally fit on test data, because there's nowhere to do it.

Data leakage: a dramatic example

Leakage means information from the test set sneaks into training, so your test score is better than real life will be. Here's a case with pure noise, where the honest answer is a coin flip:

The labels are random, so nothing can truly be learned. The leaky version still reports 73%. Out of 5,000 noise columns, a few match the labels by pure chance, including on the test rows, and selecting on all the data finds exactly those. The pipeline version selects using training rows only and gets 55%, about a coin flip, which is the truth. (make_pipeline is a shortcut that names the steps for you.)

Fitting a scaler or imputer on all rows leaks the same way, just less dramatically. The fix is always the same: split first, and put every fitted step inside the pipeline.

Watch out

Calling fit_transform on your full X before train_test_split is the most common leak in student projects. If you see fit or fit_transform on anything other than training data, stop and move that step into the pipeline.

A tumor model that is 92% accurate sounds trustworthy until you ask what the other 8% were. Telling a healthy patient they might have cancer leads to an extra scan and a scary week. Telling a cancer patient they're fine can cost their life. Accuracy counts both mistakes the same. This week you learn metrics that keep them apart, and the one setting that controls how many of each you make.

Setup: a screening model

We'll build a deliberately simple model from just two measurements, tumor radius and texture, so it makes enough mistakes to study. Run these cells in order in one notebook.

Why flip the labels? scikit-learn's metric functions treat label 1 as the positive class, meaning the thing you're trying to detect. In this dataset 1 originally means benign. Flipping makes "positive" mean "malignant," which is what a screening test looks for. Getting the positive class wrong is one of the easiest ways to report the wrong numbers, so always check which class is 1.

The confusion matrix

Every prediction falls into one of four boxes:

  • True positive (TP): malignant, predicted malignant.
  • True negative (TN): benign, predicted benign.
  • False positive (FP): benign, predicted malignant. A false alarm.
  • False negative (FN): malignant, predicted benign. A missed cancer.

Rows are the true class and columns are the predicted class, both in order 0 then 1. So the top row is the 90 benign tumors (87 called benign, 3 false alarms), and the bottom row is the 53 malignant ones (8 missed, 45 caught). .ravel() flattens the 2x2 grid in the order TN, FP, FN, TP.

To see it as a picture:

You get a 2x2 grid of colored squares with the counts written inside. The two big numbers (87 and 45) sit on the diagonal from top left to bottom right, where predictions are correct. The small off-diagonal numbers are the mistakes.

Four metrics from four numbers

  • Accuracy = (TP + TN) / everything. The share of all predictions that were right.
  • Precision = TP / (TP + FP). Of the tumors we flagged as malignant, how many really were? High precision means few false alarms.
  • Recall = TP / (TP + FN). Of the tumors that were malignant, how many did we catch? High recall means few misses. (Also called sensitivity or true positive rate.)
  • F1 = 2 × precision × recall / (precision + recall). The harmonic mean, which is only high when both are high.

Check by hand: precision = 45 / (45 + 3) = 0.938, and recall = 45 / (45 + 8) = 0.849. The model rarely raises a false alarm, but it misses about 1 cancer in 7. That weakness was hidden inside "92% accurate."

Why the harmonic mean? If precision were 1.0 and recall 0.02, the regular average would be 0.51, which sounds okay. F1 would be 0.04, which is honest about how useless that model is.

classification_report prints all of this for both classes at once:

support is how many true examples of each class there are. Macro avg averages the two classes equally, while weighted avg weights them by support, so the bigger class counts more.

The decision threshold

predict hides a choice. Logistic regression actually outputs a probability, and predict says "malignant" whenever that probability is at least 0.5. You can get the probabilities yourself and pick a different cutoff:

predict_proba returns one column per class, in the order of model.classes_ (here [0, 1]), so [:, 1] is the malignant column.

This is the precision-recall trade-off. Raise the threshold and the model only flags tumors it's very sure about: no false alarms, but 21 missed cancers. Lower it and it catches nearly everything but sends 34 healthy patients for extra tests. No threshold is "correct." You pick one based on what each mistake costs. For a first screening test, where a false alarm means another scan, 0.3 or lower is reasonable. For a spam filter, where a false positive hides a real email, you'd go higher.

Watch out

Don't choose your threshold by trying values on the test set and keeping the best one. That tunes the model on the test data, and the score you report will be too optimistic. Choose it on a separate validation split, then confirm it once on the test set. The code-along shows how.

Which metric when?

  • Recall when misses are expensive: disease screening, fraud detection, safety alerts.
  • Precision when false alarms are expensive: spam filtering, recommending a costly treatment.
  • F1 when you need one number that balances both, especially when the positive class is rare.
  • Accuracy only when classes are roughly balanced and both mistakes cost about the same.

How k-fold cross-validation works

Cut the data into k equal parts, called folds. Train on k − 1 folds and score on the one left out. Repeat k times so every fold gets a turn as the validation set. You end up with k scores.

With k = 5:

  • Round 1: train on folds 2–5, score on fold 1
  • Round 2: train on folds 1, 3, 4, 5, score on fold 2
  • ...and so on through round 5

Every row is used for validation exactly once and for training four times. Report the mean as your estimate and the standard deviation as your uncertainty.

Stratified folds

For classification, use StratifiedKFold. It keeps the class proportions about the same in every fold, which is the same reason you used stratify=y in train_test_split. Turn on shuffle=True too. Some datasets are sorted by class, and unshuffled folds of sorted data can leave a whole class out of training.

The five scores run from 0.959 to 0.993. If you had made one split and gotten fold 2, you would have reported 0.959. If you had gotten fold 4, you would have reported 0.993. The honest summary is "about 0.98, give or take 0.01."

Passing the pipeline to cross_val_score matters. The scaler is refit inside every fold, on that fold's training rows only, so no information leaks from the validation fold. If you scaled X first and cross-validated afterward, every fold's scaler would have already seen the validation rows.

Where the test set fits

Cross-validation doesn't replace your test set. A typical workflow:

  1. Split off a test set and don't touch it.
  2. Use cross-validation on the training set to compare models and settings.
  3. Score the final choice on the test set once.

On a small dataset, people sometimes cross-validate on all the data and skip the test set. That's fine for learning, but in a real project, keep the test set.

Overfitting and underfitting

A model underfits when it is too simple to capture the pattern. Training and validation scores are both low. A model overfits when it memorizes the training rows, noise included. The training score is high, the validation score is noticeably lower, and that gap is the warning sign.

A decision tree makes this easy to see, because max_depth sets how complex it can get. validation_curve cross-validates the model once for each value of one hyperparameter and returns training and validation scores:

Both arrays have shape (n_values, n_folds), so .mean(axis=1) averages over the folds. If you plotted depth on the x-axis, you would see the training line climb steadily to 1.0. The validation line rises to a peak at depth 4 and then sags a little. To the left of the peak the tree underfits. To the right, it is memorizing: perfect on the rows it trained on, and no better (actually slightly worse) on new ones. The best setting is around the peak, where validation is highest. Training is not the score to maximize.

Learning curves: would more data help?

A learning curve fixes the model and changes how much training data it gets. It answers a practical question: should you go collect more data, or change the model?

The unlimited-depth tree scores a perfect 1.000 on its training data at every size. That's overfitting in its purest form. Validation keeps climbing as data grows, but it flattens out after about 250 rows. On a plot, the two lines would still be far apart at the right edge.

How to read the shapes:

  • Big gap that keeps shrinking: high variance. More data helps, and so does a simpler or regularized model.
  • Both lines low and close together: high bias, so the model is underfitting. More data won't fix it. Use a more flexible model or better features.
  • Both lines high and close together: you're in good shape.

Watch out

A tiny standard deviation doesn't make a score trustworthy if the folds leak. Make sure every preprocessing step lives inside the pipeline you pass to cross_val_score, validation_curve, or learning_curve.

Common mistakes

  • Reporting the best fold instead of the mean.
  • Leaving out the ± std, so nobody can tell whether a 0.005 difference between two models means anything.
  • Using plain KFold without shuffling on data sorted by class.
  • Tuning max_depth by looking at test-set scores. Use the validation curve for that.

The keys are test_accuracy, test_precision, and so on, plus fit_time and score_time. All of them are computed on the same five fits, which is cheaper than calling cross_val_score four times. "My random forest got 97% and my logistic regression got 96%, so the forest wins." Before you believe a claim like that, ask three questions. Were both models scored on the same rows? Was the preprocessing fit separately inside each fold? Is a one-point gap bigger than the noise? This week is about making comparisons that hold up when someone asks those questions.

The three model families

  • Decision tree: a flowchart of yes/no questions on features. Easy to explain, needs no scaling, and overfits readily (you saw this last week).
  • Random forest: hundreds of trees, each trained on a random resample of the rows and considering a random subset of features at each split. Averaging their votes cancels much of the individual trees' variance. It needs no scaling and is usually strong right out of the box.
  • Logistic regression: a weighted sum of features pushed through a sigmoid. It's fast, gives well-behaved probabilities, and its coefficients are interpretable. It does need scaled features, and it can only draw straight-line (linear) boundaries unless you engineer features.

None of these is always best. You find out by testing them on your data.

Rules for a fair comparison

  1. Same folds. Create one StratifiedKFold object with a fixed random_state and pass it to every model.
  2. Everything inside a pipeline. Scaling, imputing, and encoding are refit in each fold for every model.
  3. Same metric, chosen before you look at results.
  4. Include the baseline, so you know what "good" means on this dataset.

ROC AUC measures how well a model ranks positives above negatives across every possible threshold. 0.5 is random guessing and 1.0 is perfect ranking. It's a good metric for comparing models, and you'll choose a specific threshold separately.

Because every model saw identical folds, you can compare them fold by fold. Logistic regression beats the forest on 4 of 5 folds, which is stronger evidence than comparing two means. The tree is clearly behind. Every model is wrapped in a Pipeline with a step named "model", even the ones with no preprocessing. That consistent naming pays off when you tune.

Hyperparameters vs. parameters

Parameters are learned from data: a tree's split points, logistic regression's coefficients. Hyperparameters are settings you choose before training: max_depth, n_estimators, C. Tuning means searching for hyperparameters that give the best cross-validated score.

Grid search

GridSearchCV tries every combination in a grid and cross-validates each one. Inside a pipeline, you name a hyperparameter as step name + two underscores + parameter name, so model__C means "the C of the step called model."

After the search, refit=True (the default) retrains the best pipeline on all of X_train, so search itself becomes your final model. cv_results_ holds the full results table. Load it into a pandas DataFrame to sort and inspect it. Notice that C = 0.1 and C = 1 tie. The search picks the first one listed, and the differences between most of these settings are well inside one standard deviation.

Watch out

Writing {"C": [...]} for a pipeline raises ValueError: Invalid parameter 'C' for estimator Pipeline(...). The pipeline doesn't have a C; its model step does. Run pipe.get_params().keys() to list every valid name.

Random search

A grid grows quickly. Four hyperparameters with five values each is 625 combinations, and at 5 folds each that's 3,125 fits. RandomizedSearchCV samples a fixed number of combinations (n_iter) from lists or distributions. Random search usually finds a near-best setting in a fraction of the fits, because typically only one or two hyperparameters really matter, and random sampling tries many distinct values of each one.

randint(50, 200) samples whole numbers from 50 to 199. For a hyperparameter like C that spans orders of magnitude, use scipy.stats.loguniform(1e-3, 1e2) so that 0.001–0.01 gets as many samples as 10–100. n_jobs=-1 uses every CPU core. Expect this search to take 10–30 seconds in Colab.

Why best_score_ is a little optimistic

Every search reports the highest cross-validated score it found. If you try 10 settings, one of them will look good partly by luck. Picking the maximum of several noisy numbers biases the result upward. Two defenses:

  • The test set, used once. It played no part in the search, so it gives an unbiased check on the final choice. The 0.9940 above is the number to report.
  • Nested cross-validation. Put the whole search inside an outer CV loop. The inner loop tunes, and the outer folds score the tuned model on data the search never saw:

Nested CV estimates how well the whole procedure (search plus refit) works. It doesn't produce one final model. On small datasets where a test set would be tiny, it's the most honest number you can give.

load_digits contains 1,797 tiny 8×8 grayscale images of handwritten digits. Each image is flattened into 64 pixel values from 0 to 16. Ten balanced classes and a fair amount of data make it a good arena: different model families really do perform differently here, and tuning moves the numbers.

You'll build a notebook that runs a shootout: three model families, each tuned with a search, all scored on identical folds, ranked on a leaderboard, with one final test-set check of the winner. Run each step as its own cell. The forest search takes 10–30 seconds.

Step 1: Split once, fold once

The 360 test images go into a metaphorical vault. Every search below gets the same cv object, so each candidate setting of every model is scored on exactly the same five sets of validation images.

Step 2: Define one search per model family

Each model sits in a Pipeline whose estimator step is named "model". That way every grid uses the same model__... naming.

Why each search looks the way it does:

  • Tree: two small lists give 4 × 3 = 12 combinations, which is cheap enough for a full grid.
  • Logistic: only C matters much here, so it gets one log-spaced list. The scaler lives inside the pipeline, so it's refit on each fold's training images.
  • Forest: three hyperparameters, one of them a range of integers. A full grid would be hundreds of combinations. Six random samples keeps the run short while you learn. Raise it in a real project.

Accuracy is a fine metric here because the ten classes are almost exactly balanced. On imbalanced data you would pick something else (next week).

Step 3: Run the searches and build a leaderboard

best_index_ points at the winning row of cv_results_, so you can pull out the std of the best setting too. best_score_ gives you only the mean.

What the leaderboard says:

  • The single tree is far behind, about 12 points below the others. Even tuned, one tree on raw pixels is too unstable.
  • The forest leads logistic regression by about half a point, which is smaller than the forest's own standard deviation (1.1 points). That's a near tie, not a clear win.
  • Logistic regression is that close while being much faster and simpler. In a real project you might reasonably pick it instead, and the trade-off is worth stating out loud. Here we follow the leaderboard so you can see the whole procedure.

Step 4: Look inside one search

The leaderboard shows only each family's best setting. cv_results_ shows every setting, and it often teaches you more.

Depth 15 and unlimited depth tie exactly: the trees stop growing before they reach 15 levels, so the two settings build the same trees. The two depth-10 rows both show 0.8462 after rounding, but their unrounded scores differ slightly, which is why their ranks differ. When rows are this close, choose the simpler or more stable one (the smaller std) rather than chasing the fourth decimal.

Tip

Every searched hyperparameter gets a column named param_<name>. Sorting by rank_test_score is the quickest way to see the top settings.

Step 5: Open the vault once

best_estimator_ is the winning pipeline, already refit on all 1,437 training images. The test accuracy is about 1.6 points under the CV estimate. Part of that is the optimism you read about in the Notes: the forest's score is the best of six tries, and the best of several noisy scores tends to run high. Part is ordinary test-set noise, since each image is worth 0.28 points.

Watch out

Don't score the logistic model on the test set too and switch if it does better. The moment you pick between models using test scores, the test set is part of your selection process and its score is no longer unbiased. If you need another opinion, use nested CV on the training set.

Suppose 1 transaction in 20 is fraud. A model that says "not fraud" every single time is 95% accurate, catches zero fraud, and would get you fired. When one class is rare, the usual scoreboard stops working. This week covers what to measure instead, two ways to push a model toward the rare class, how to find where a model fails, and how to write all of it up so a reader can trust it.

The accuracy trap, in numbers

make_classification with weights=[0.95, 0.05] creates data where about 5% of rows are positive. Let's cross-validate a baseline, a plain logistic regression, and one with class_weight="balanced":

Read across the rows:

  • The dummy's accuracy is 0.945, only 2 points behind the real model. Accuracy can hardly tell them apart.
  • Balanced accuracy averages the recall of each class, so the dummy drops to 0.5. That's a much more honest gap.
  • Average precision (the area under the precision–recall curve) summarizes ranking quality on the rare class across every threshold. Its floor is the positive rate (0.055), not 0.5, which makes it much harder to flatter than ROC AUC on rare classes.
  • Plain logistic regression is very precise (0.987) but finds only 39% of positives.

Fix 1: class_weight="balanced"

This option makes each positive row count about 17 times as much in the loss (the ratio of negatives to positives), so mistakes on the rare class cost more. Recall jumps to 0.795, but precision falls to 0.186: for every true positive flagged, about four false alarms come along. F1 went down, and average precision dipped too.

Class weighting mostly shifts where the model draws the line. It rarely makes the model better at telling the classes apart. Tree models and forests take the same class_weight argument.

Fix 2: Choose the threshold on purpose

predict uses a probability cutoff of 0.5, which is rarely the right choice for a rare class. To choose a better one without leaking, get out-of-fold probabilities with cross_val_predict, so every row's probability comes from a model that never trained on it, and then search the precision–recall curve:

precision_recall_curve returns one more precision/recall value than thresholds, which is why the code slices with [:-1]. Two good ways to choose:

  • Maximize F1 when misses and false alarms matter about equally. Here, a threshold of 0.253 lifts F1 from 0.552 to 0.635.
  • Meet a requirement, such as "catch at least 70% of fraud," and then take the threshold with the best precision that still meets it. That depends on a business or safety decision, so write it down.

Watch out

The threshold is a hyperparameter. Choose it with out-of-fold predictions on the training set, then check it once on the test set. Choosing it by looking at test predictions leaks, just like tuning C on the test set would.

Resampling, such as oversampling the rare class with SMOTE, is another option. It lives in the separate imbalanced-learn package (pip install imbalanced-learn), and you don't need it for this course. If you try it, the resampling must happen inside the pipeline so that only training folds are resampled.

Error analysis across slices

One overall score can hide a group the model fails badly. To find it, take out-of-fold predictions, bucket a meaningful feature, and compute errors per bucket. Here, breast cancer tumors are grouped by size, with malignant treated as the positive class (in this dataset's labels, 0 means malignant):

pd.qcut makes equal-sized buckets. The overall error rate is about 2%, but medium tumors have double that, and 5 of the 9 missed cancers are there. That makes sense: small tumors are almost all benign and large ones almost all malignant, so the hard, ambiguous cases sit in the middle. Keep the counts in the table, though. Six errors is a small number, so call it a lead worth investigating, not a proven law.

The one-page model report

Your work is only as useful as the reader's understanding of it. A short report needs these parts:

Good limitation statements are specific: "Medium-sized tumors have twice the error rate; all data comes from one hospital study; the model has not been tested on other imaging equipment." A vague one like "the model may not be perfect" tells the reader nothing.

Screening tools are judged by different rules than contest leaderboards. A tool that flags tumors for a specialist to review should almost never let a malignant one slip through, and it can afford some false alarms, because a human looks at every flag. You'll build exactly that kind of model today, using the breast cancer dataset with malignant as the positive class. Each step is one notebook cell.

Step 1: Data with the right positive class

scikit-learn's metrics treat label 1 as positive, and in this dataset 1 means benign. Flipping the labels makes "recall" mean "share of cancers caught." Get this wrong and every number in your report answers the wrong question.

Step 2: Do class weights help here?

At a 37/63 split the imbalance is mild, and weighting doesn't raise recall at all: it only costs a little precision. Average precision, which measures ranking quality regardless of threshold, is identical for the two logistic models. The forest ranks a bit worse. So the honest choice is the plain logistic regression, and the recall target will come from the threshold instead of from weighting. Testing whether a fix helps before using it is a big part of evaluating well.

Step 3: Choose a threshold for 99% recall

oof holds out-of-fold probabilities for the 426 training rows, so each probability comes from a model that never saw that tumor. Among the thresholds that reach 99% recall, the code picks the one with the best precision.

The trade-off is plain: lowering the cutoff from 0.5 to 0.095 cuts misses on the training folds from 4 to 1 (159 malignant × 2.5% vs. × 0.6%). In exchange, precision drops from 99% to 85%, so roughly one flag in seven is a false alarm. For a tool that sends cases to a specialist, that's a reasonable deal. For a tool that orders surgery, it would not be. The threshold is a values decision, and the code just makes the cost visible.

Step 4: Slice the mistakes

Overall numbers hide groups. Let's bucket tumors by mean texture (variation in gray levels on the scan) and count both kinds of error per bucket, using the out-of-fold predictions at the new threshold:

The false-alarm rate is divided by the number of benign tumors in each bucket, because only benign tumors can be false alarms. Benign tumors with high texture get flagged 22% of the time, four times the rate in the low bucket. In practice, that means patients with high-texture benign tumors would be called back for review more often. That's worth knowing, and worth putting in the report.

Tip

Using out-of-fold training predictions for slicing gives you 426 rows to analyze instead of 143. Slicing doesn't choose anything, so it's safe. If you change the model because of a slice, though, re-run Steps 2–3 so the choice is still validated.

Step 5: One look at the test set

Test recall (0.962) came in under the 0.99 target. With 53 malignant test tumors, one miss costs about 1.9 points, so two misses instead of one moves recall from 0.981 to 0.962. Don't lower the threshold again to fix this: that would be tuning on the test set. Report it as it is.

Step 6: Generate the report from the numbers

Typing numbers into a report by hand is how typos and stale results sneak in. Build the report with an f-string so it always matches the code:

Notice what the report doesn't claim. It doesn't say "96% accurate," and it doesn't hide that test recall missed the target. It also says plainly how the model should and shouldn't be used.

Rare classes make bad evaluations look good. Each exercise below gives you a habit that keeps you honest: check the baseline, test whether a fix helps, write down why a threshold is what it is, and look for the group where the model struggles. Exercise 1: The accuracy trap

Generate make_classification(n_samples=2000, weights=[0.9, 0.1], random_state=0), make a stratified 75/25 split (random_state=0), and fit DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"). Print its test accuracy, balanced accuracy, and recall for class 1. Write one sentence you could say to someone who claims "89% accuracy" is a good result on this data.

Show solution

"A model that always says 'no' already gets 89.6% here and finds none of the positives, so 89% accuracy means nothing until we see recall or balanced accuracy." make_classification also flips about 1% of labels at random by default, which is why the positive rate is 10.4% instead of exactly 10%.

Show solution

Weighting more than triples recall, but nearly 9 of every 10 flags become false alarms, and F1 falls. If missing a positive is very costly (for example, a safety check followed by a cheap human review), the balanced tree may be the right tool. If every flag triggers something expensive, it isn't. The metric you optimize must follow from the use case, so state the use case first.

Your team can only handle alerts that are right at least half the time. Using the data from Exercise 2, get out-of-fold probabilities from RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0) and find the threshold with the highest recall among those with precision ≥ 0.5. Compare it with the default 0.5 cutoff.

At 0.5 the forest is very precise but finds less than a quarter of positives. Dropping to 0.18 nearly triples recall while staying inside the team's limit. The forest's probabilities are averaged tree votes, and on rare classes they rarely get near 0.5, which is one more reason never to trust the default cutoff.

The cost-based cutoff saves about 23% of the total cost. np.isclose is used because np.arange with decimal steps produces values like 0.5000000000000001, so thresholds == 0.5 could fail. A cost table is the easiest threshold justification to defend in a report: the reader can disagree with your costs, but they can see exactly how you got the number.

The tuned threshold still clearly beats both alternatives. Newer scikit-learn versions (1.5+) include TunedThresholdClassifierCV, which automates this pattern, but writing it once by hand shows you exactly what it protects against.

Most machine learning projects end with a model. Yours ends with a verdict: a report that tells a reader whether a model is good enough to use, how sure you are, where it fails, and what it should never be used for. The model is part of the evidence. The reasoning is what you're graded on.

The brief

Choose a public or bundled classification dataset and produce a notebook plus a short written report that includes:

  1. A clear decision. Who would use the model, and what action does a prediction trigger?
  2. A baseline. A DummyClassifier scored with the same folds and metrics as everything else.
  3. At least two tuned models from different families (for example, logistic regression and a random forest), each inside a leak-free Pipeline and tuned with GridSearchCV or RandomizedSearchCV.
  4. Cross-validated metrics reported as mean ± std, on shared folds, using metrics that suit your class balance.
  5. A justified threshold, chosen from out-of-fold training predictions using a stated rule: a recall target, a precision floor, a cost table, or best F1.
  6. One held-out test evaluation, done once, at the end.
  7. Slice-based error analysis. At least one feature bucketed into groups, with error counts and rates per group.
  8. A written recommendation with limitations. Use, don't use, or use with conditions, and what you didn't test.

You have three weeks: planning now, building in milestones next, then checking and presenting.

Picking a dataset

A good capstone dataset has a few hundred rows or more, a target you can explain in one sentence, and at least one feature that makes a meaningful slice (size, age, region, amount). Run this quick scout on the bundled candidates to compare their sizes and class balance:

Ideas, roughly from easier to harder:

  • Breast cancer screening (load_breast_cancer). Binary, mildly imbalanced, with natural slices by tumor size or texture. A strong default if you're unsure. Use a different slice and threshold rule than the class examples.
  • "Is it a 9?" detector (load_digits, target == 9). Turning ten classes into one-vs-rest gives you a real 10% imbalance. Slice by ink amount (the sum of pixel values) or by which digit a false alarm actually was.
  • Wine cultivar classifier (load_wine). Three classes, so you'll use macro F1 and per-class recall. It's small, which makes the ± std discussion interesting. For the threshold, describe how you'd handle low-confidence predictions (for example, "send to a human if the top probability is below 0.6").
  • Synthetic rare-event detector (make_classification with weights=[0.97, 0.03]). You control the imbalance exactly, but the features have no real meaning, so your slices and limitations must say so. Best for students who want to dig into threshold and cost analysis.
  • Public OpenML datasets via sklearn.datasets.fetch_openml, which needs an internet connection the first time. Examples: "credit-g" (good vs. bad credit, 30% bad) or "diabetes" (the Pima diabetes data, 35% positive). These have categorical features or messy values, so you'll use the ColumnTransformer and SimpleImputer skills from earlier weeks. Pass as_frame=True and check the target column's name and values before you do anything else.

Watch out

Avoid datasets where a feature is the answer in disguise, such as an ID that was assigned after diagnosis or a "follow-up date" that only exists for positive cases. If one feature gets near-perfect accuracy by itself, suspect leakage before you celebrate.

Write the plan before the code

Spend this session on a one-page plan. Fill in every line. A blank line now usually means a stuck afternoon later.

A few guidelines for the hardest lines:

  • Primary metric. For balanced data, accuracy or ROC AUC is fine for comparing models. For a 10% positive class, prefer average precision or F1, and always show recall. For multiclass, use macro F1.
  • Threshold rule. Tie it to the decision. "A specialist reviews every flag, so I want recall ≥ 0.98" is a rule. "0.3 looked good" is not.
  • Slice features. Pick something a real user would care about. A slice that reveals nothing is still a valid result: "error rates were similar across all three size groups" is a finding.

Budget your compute

Count fits before you launch a search. Settings × folds + 1 refit, as in Week 5. A random forest with 300 trees on a few thousand rows is fine for 10–20 random-search iterations in Colab. A 500-setting grid is not. If a search takes more than a few minutes, lower n_iter or n_estimators while you develop, and save the larger run for the end.

Timeline

Session Goal
This week Dataset chosen, plan written, data loaded and explored
Next week Milestones 1–5: baseline, tuned models, threshold, test score, slices
Final week Checks, polished report, 5-minute presentation

What "done" looks like

Someone who has never seen your notebook can read your one-page report and answer: should this model be used, under what conditions, and what could go wrong? If they can, you've done the job.

Milestone 0: Settings

Milestone 2: Baseline

DummyClassifier(strategy="prior") predicts the class proportions, and its average precision equals the positive rate (0.374 here). Every later number must be compared against this one.

Every search used the same cv object, so cv_results_["split0_test_score"] through split4_test_score are directly comparable fold by fold, with no extra fitting needed. In the example, logistic regression edges out the forest (0.993 vs. 0.991), but the gap is much smaller than either std. That's a near tie, and your report should say so. When results tie, the simpler or faster model is a reasonable tiebreaker. Write down whichever reason you use.

Check: the board shows mean ± std and per-fold scores for each model, and you've written one sentence on whether the gap is meaningful.

A surprising number of excellent-looking capstones fall apart under one question from the audience: "What happens if you shuffle the labels?" This lesson is about asking those questions yourself first. Then you'll polish the report and practice the presentation.

Four sanity checks

Run these against your final pipeline, using training data only. They take a minute and catch the most common reasons a result is too good to be true.

What each check tells you:

  1. Shared rows. If the same row is in both train and test, the model is graded on something it memorized. Datasets assembled from several files often contain duplicates. Fix: drop duplicates before splitting.
  2. Shuffled labels. Once the labels are shuffled, there's no real pattern left, so an honest pipeline must fall to roughly the baseline. Here it drops from 0.993 to 0.400, near the 0.374 positive rate. If your shuffled score stays high, something in X is leaking the answer or your preprocessing is happening outside the pipeline.
  3. Fold-seed stability. The CV mean varies only from 0.993 to 0.995 across five different fold shuffles, so you can report it with confidence. If your range is wide, report the range and avoid fine distinctions between models.
  4. Single-feature check. If one feature alone scores near 1.0, ask whether it would really be available at prediction time. Here worst perimeter reaches 0.964 alone. That's high, but it makes sense, since large tumors are more often malignant, and it's still clearly below the full model. Mention this in your report: it tells the reader that tumor size carries much of the signal.

Watch out

Don't run these checks on the test set. They're part of development, and any check that leads you to change the model has to use training data only.

Polishing the report

Your report should fit on one page. Go through your draft and make these edits:

  • Lead with the recommendation. The first two sentences should say what the model is for and whether you recommend it. Details come after.
  • Every number has context. "AP 0.993 ± 0.006 (baseline 0.374)" beats "AP 0.993". "2 missed of 42 malignant test tumors" beats "recall 0.952".
  • Round sensibly. Three decimals for metrics and two significant figures for thresholds. More digits than the std justifies is false precision.
  • Show the trade-off. One or two sentences on what the threshold gains and costs ("catches 97% of malignant tumors; about 1 in 9 flags is a false alarm").
  • Name limitations specifically. Data source, time period, groups not represented, weak slices, small test counts. Each one should change how a reader uses the model.
  • Describe plots in words. If you include a validation curve or a precision–recall curve, the caption should say what to notice ("validation F1 peaks at depth 4 and falls after"). A grader skimming the page should get the point without studying the axes.

Presenting in five minutes

Use this structure. It mirrors the report, so you won't need extra slides or notes.

  1. The decision (30 s). Who uses the model and what a positive prediction triggers.
  2. The data (30 s). Source, size, positive rate, and the one quirk you had to handle.
  3. The contest (1 min). Baseline vs. your two tuned models on shared folds, with mean ± std. Say whether the winner's lead is meaningful.
  4. The threshold (1 min). Your rule, the chosen value, and the trade-off it creates.
  5. The test and the slices (1 min). The single test result, and the slice where the model is weakest.
  6. The verdict (1 min). Recommendation, the most important limitation, and what you'd do with more time.

Practice it once out loud with a timer. Expect these questions and have one-sentence answers ready: "How many times did you look at the test set?", "Why that threshold?", "What happens with shuffled labels?", "Would this work on data from somewhere else?"

Tip

If a result surprised you, such as a simpler model winning or a slice showing no difference, say so. A surprise you explain sounds like real analysis, while a perfect story sounds rehearsed.

Grading checklist

Check each item before you submit. Each is worth the points shown, for 100 in total.

  • Problem framing (10). The decision, the user, the positive class, and which error is worse are stated up front.
  • Baseline (5). A DummyClassifier scored on the same folds and metric.
  • Leak-free pipelines (15). All preprocessing is inside Pipeline/ColumnTransformer, and the shuffled-label check falls to near baseline.
  • Two or more tuned model families (15). Grid or random search with sensible ranges and correct step__param names, and best settings not stuck at a range edge.
  • Fair comparison (10). Shared folds, mean ± std, and a sentence on whether the gap is meaningful.
  • Justified threshold (10). Chosen from out-of-fold training predictions with a stated rule tied to the use case.
  • Single test evaluation (5). Done once, reported as-is, with counts.
  • Slice-based error analysis (10). At least one bucketed feature, with counts and rates, and an interpretation.
  • Report and limitations (15). One page, recommendation first, specific limitations, and numbers consistent with the notebook.
  • Reproducibility and presentation (5). The notebook runs top to bottom with fixed seeds, and the talk fits in five minutes.

Before you submit, restart the runtime and choose Run all. If any cell fails or any number changes, fix it before you hand in. A notebook that runs top to bottom from a fresh start is the strongest proof that your results are real.
